title: Berlin Pride attack suspect shot and killed during police operation
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police at an allotment in the Spandau borough in Berlin's west on SundayByJake LaphamThe man suspected of carrying
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police at an allotment in the Spandau borough in Berlin's west on SundayByJake LaphamThe man suspected of carrying out what authorities say was likely an "Islamist terror attack" at Berlin Pride has been shot and killed by police.Officers opened fire when Abdul Ballout, a 21-year-old German citizen with Lebanese heritage, rushed at them with a knife in Spandau, a western borough of Berlin. It brought an end to a massive manhunt that was launched after a white van was driven into a crowd of people near Tiergarten park just before 22:00 (local time) on Saturday evening, killing one woman and injuring at least 29 others. Police say following the ramming, several people were injured in a stabbing attack.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Investigators at the scene in Tiergarten park on SundaySpeaking to reporters on Sunday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said evidence pointed to it being an "Islamist terror attack"."We are dealing with a suspected perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene," Dobrindt said.A statement released by the Berlin public prosecutor's office revealed further details about Ballout's criminal history.In May 2025, prosecutors said he travelled via Turkey to Lebanon, with the intention of joining the Islamic State group (IS) in Syria. While in Lebanon he allegedly made contact with several individuals he believed were members of IS.He was arrested in Lebanon in July 2025 and sentenced to three months in prison for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict.Then in November 2025 he returned to Germany where he was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and held in pre-trial detention.In May this year, he was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state". The decision was deferred for six months and he was placed under the supervision of a parole officer. He was previously convicted of assault and robbery in 2022, and of robbing a victim of headphones in 2020.Image source, Polizei BerlinImage caption, Abdul Ballout was shot and killed in a police operation on Sunday afternoonDobrindt said Germany's threat level would be raised following the attack, while other states were also being briefed about the attack and advised to review their security measures for major events.On Sunday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the scene of the attack in Tiergarten park. He later spoke outside a church service that paid tribute to victims, where he pledged to "defend the freedom and openness of our lives"."These extremists have no place in our society," he said, adding that Germany would not allow the "poison of terrorism" to affect its society.Berlin police have said people were hit on Ahornsteig street, which is a long path stretching across the Tiergarten park, largely in a forested area.Meanwhile, German media say those injured in the attack are no longer in a life-threatening condition. Saturday's attack shattered the joy and revelry of Berlin's Christopher Street Day, where hundreds of thousands spill onto the city streets for one of Europe's most famous Pride events. Christopher Street Day commemorates the first known uprising among the LGBT community in New York City in 1969 at the Stonewall Inn, which is located on Christopher Street. A clean-up even due to take place at Tiergarten park and a breakfast market scheduled for Sunday morning were both cancelled following the attack.Later in the day, some members of the LGBT community returned to the iconic Brandenburg Gate for an impromptu vigil. Speakers condemned extremism in all its manifestations, but they also criticised the government for a lack of support, singling out recent budget cuts for queer organisations.Armin Duenhoelter from Wolfsburg, who works as a drag artist, was backstage at the main stage when the attack happened.He told Agency France-Presse that he was still shocked but vowed to be back for next year's pride celebration."We won't let it beat us down," he said.Image source, Omer Messinger/Getty ImagesImage caption, Mourners gather near the Brandenburg Gate on Sunday

schema.headline: Berlin Pride attack suspect shot and killed during police operation

title: Meghan calls Prince Harry 'a charmer' during MasterChef Australia appearance
description: Early on in the episode, Meghan was asked what her favourite dish is to make at home.She said it was "a tough one because I have a lot of palettes to
body: Early on in the episode, Meghan was asked what her favourite dish is to make at home.She said it was "a tough one because I have a lot of palettes to appease", with her British-born husband favouring "meat, potatoes and cream sauce" while she preferred grilled fish.Their two children, Archie and Lilibet, often help with meal preparation and are "great eaters", she said."We're really lucky on that front," she added.She then urged the chefs to cook something they felt connected to. "What's the story behind it?" she asked them.When Prince Harry dialled in later on during the episode, Meghan told them: "My husband's here," prompting cheers and shocked faces from contestants and spectators."I wish you could try these, these dishes are fantastic," she told him, before showing him the food. He signed off by telling her to go and enjoy, adding: "Very sorry to disturb you."The duchess’s appearance on the latest season of the show was well received by Hello Magazine, external, which shared a video of the episode online and complimented Meghan for the way she interacted with the chefs."The Duchess of Sussex gave personal time calls to all the contestants, proving that she's always so effortlessly elegant," it wrote.Writing in The Sunday Times, external, Charlotte Ivers was less impressed, saying her appearance on the show "told us nothing about what she likes or who even will leave the competition".Social media users were also split, with one viewer writing that Meghan was "warm, gracious and a delight to watch" while another called Prince Harry's cameo appearance "cringe".

schema.headline: Meghan calls Prince Harry 'a charmer' during MasterChef Australia appearance

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Gymnast Reuben Ward goes from Glasgow dreamer to Scotland gold medallist
description: There was a sense beforehand that Ward could contend here. A bronze maybe. Perhaps even a silver depending how things go. His team-mates privately mad
body: There was a sense beforehand that Ward could contend here. A bronze maybe. Perhaps even a silver depending how things go. His team-mates privately made noises that, should everything fall in his favour, gold could be within reach. They had seen him in training, and performed alongside him in the team event on Friday, where Scotland finished fourth. They knew he was in a good place.Ward sat seventh after the floor exercise, but streaked into the lead after a splendid performance on the pommel - routinely his strongest event. He retained that advantage after the rings - by which point assorted Team Scotland officials and members of the Scottish media had arrived in dribs and drabs, with the sniff of a gold in the air.Ward's vault had been compromised in the team event by a slight issue in his run up - he had to adapt it on the fly and could only execute two twists - but he nailed it this time, performing three to go into the final two rotations top of the standings.A strong showing in the parallel bars - and a judicious Team Scotland appeal to add an extra 0.100 - maintained his lead at 0.550, meaning he needed to keep his shape in the horizontal bar to clinch gold.Ward did that and more. As he stuck his landing, his coach Jake Seager fell to his knees celebrating before the two embraced. It wasn't official yet, but they knew."I like to imagine the best scenario possible and that was winning," added Ward when asked what he was thinking as his head hit the pillow on Saturday night."It kept me awake a little bit because I was picturing it and feeling the emotions. But this beat the expectations by a mile. "Falling short on Friday was heartbreaking and I'm just so overwhelmed, man. I can barely put words together."It could get even better. He goes on the floor and pommel on Monday, and is a real medal contender in the later.His celebrations will have to wait for now, but by Tuesday, Ward could well be getting up to all sorts of capers in Glasgow with his Scotland team-mates."Tonight looks like eating hotel food and probably getting a pretty bad night's sleep," he said. "Then I'll come in tomorrow, and try to relax and hit my routine. "On Tuesday, after the competition, I'll celebrate big time with the team, with my boys. I love them so much and them coming to see me at the end when I was going around of the arena was special."I'm hoping we'll get to experience a bit of Glasgow.. "

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Gymnast Reuben Ward goes from Glasgow dreamer to Scotland gold medallist

title: Primark cuts prices as it feels pressure from Shein and Temu
description: "Primark isn't as cheap any more."It is something I keep hearing shoppers say when I ask them whether they shop at the fast-fashion giant."It's defini
body: "Primark isn't as cheap any more."It is something I keep hearing shoppers say when I ask them whether they shop at the fast-fashion giant."It's definitely got more expensive," says 19-year-old student Eshal Malik as she browses the jewellery at Primark with a friend.But that might be about to change. Primark said on Monday that it was lowering prices on hundreds of clothing items, including jeans, jumpers and socks."It's the kind of headline you'd expect from M&S or Next," says retail analyst Natalie Berg, explaining that price cuts like this from such a low-cost retailer are surprising."You don't want to join a race to the bottom," she says. "But when Shein is selling dresses for £3, you've got to respond, right?"Primark, which has more than 190 UK stores, has been experiencing a drop in like-for-like sales, a key measure in the retail industry.Increases to the price of fabric, minimum wages, shipping and energy costs and a focus on higher standards overall has contributed to the rising price of clothes for the likes of Primark in recent years.The announcement of price cuts comes ahead of parent company Associated British Foods' plan to spin off the business onto the London stock market next year.The level of competition among fashion retailers has "evolved dramatically" over the past few years, and Chinese online marketplaces Shein and Temu are now competing for Primark's customers, says Berg.But there is also competition from other online retailers like TikTok Shop and Vinted, she says.By slashing prices on some core items, Primark is likely hoping to woo shoppers with low-cost staples, in the same way that supermarkets attract customers with cheap milk and bananas, Berg says.Temu and Shein have been able to undercut traditional retailers like Primark because they do not pay for physical locations, most of their packages are exempt from import duties – though this exemption is set to end in October 2028, external - and they have an efficient operating model that leaves them with little unsold stock, says Berg.Currently low Shein prices are seen as the new baseline, Berg says. And they are luring in younger shoppers. According to Mintel research from July 2025, 32% of women aged 16-34 who buy clothes online said they had shopped at Shein during the previous year. Low prices, abundant discount codes and seemingly endless pages of products all feed into its attraction.Primark, in contrast, has a click and collect service but does not offer delivery - a decision it has previously said was a "deliberate choice to streamline operations and pass the savings directly to customers".Fast fashion is a term coined to describe the rapid turnover of fashion trends with cheap, mass-produced clothing. The practice has an environmental impact, using a lot of natural resources and creating greenhouse gases which are responsible for climate change.Overall, the fashion industry is responsible for around 8% of global emissions, according to the United Nations, external, which is more than aviation and shipping combined.Critics of Shein have called for a boycott of the global behemoth over the environmental impact of fast fashion, working conditions in its Chinese factories, and the sale of childlike sex dolls on its website.Allegations surrounding the sale of the dolls first came to light from France's anti-fraud office in November 2025. Shein at the time promised to co-operate fully.Some shoppers think better value for money can be found elsewhere on the High Street.Isobel Guffick, 30, from Staffordshire, feels Sainsbury's Tu range has greater quality clothes for similar prices. It is "really good for basics", she says.To save money, she also buys clothes secondhand where possible, from charity shops, car boot sales and sites like Vinted. She visits charity shops every week and loves the "treasure hunt" feel of finding a bargain.Getting a couple of pounds off a jumper or a pair of jeans might not seem like a lot to a customer, but for a shop with tight margins like Primark, how might this affect the business?"Our business model and focus on buying at scale and keeping costs low helps us to offer the prices we do, but we don't compromise on quality or ethics to do that," a Primark spokesperson told BBC News. In its latest annual report, it said that about 85% of its products are £10 or less.Crucially, the new lower prices do not cover everything Primark sells. McCusker describes the price reductions as a marketing exercise designed to bring in more shoppers - and says that even if they are drawn in by the lower prices of jeans or jumpers, they'll probably end up putting other items in their basket, too."Primark is known for that impulse nature," she explains.One big issue for some fashion retailers is having big piles of leftover stock that has to be discounted heavily so they can shift it. Primark will be expecting that the price changes "will help them shift stock, meaning they don't have to discount too much any further," says AJ Bell analyst Russ Mould.Ultimately analysts think Primark's new pricing is in response to a highly competitive retail environment."When it comes to staying relevant to customers today, you have to offer value for money," Berg says. "Especially if you are meant to be the value fashion retailer in the UK, you have to deliver on that promise."

schema.headline: Primark cuts prices as it feels pressure from Shein and Temu

title: Emmerdale makers seek forever home for soap village in Leeds
description: The makers of TV drama Emmerdale hope to continue filming on their village set at  a site in Leeds after seeking permission from the council.ITV Studi
body: The makers of TV drama Emmerdale hope to continue filming on their village set at  a site in Leeds after seeking permission from the council.ITV Studios has applied to Leeds City Council to remain at the farm site in Harewood which the show has occupied since 1997.Current planning permission allows for the location, which includes the Woolpack pub and Burden Head Farm, to be used until next year.If granted, consent from council planners would allow the site, which is popular with tourists, to be used on a permanent basis.A planning report said the set provided a variety of exterior views and was used for more than 260 episodes each year.It said: "The Emmerdale Village Production Set provides a facility which adapts to the ever-changing needs of production."These could be planned changes for certain storylines or even immediate changes due to weather conditions, cast availability or other scheduling challenges."ITV said continued use of the set was needed to depict farming life and the Yorkshire countryside, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.Interior and exterior scenes were filmed at the Harewood site, while studio space on Kirkstall Road was used for some indoor sets, including the Woolpack.The report said: "Emmerdale Village was designed to include everything a typical rural village would have, including a village hall, café, church, residential dwellings and more."Current planning permission would expire on 3 June 2027, with a condition requiring the site to be restored to its original condition within six months.A full planning application is out for consultation until 13 August.

schema.headline: Emmerdale makers seek forever home for soap village in Leeds

title: Tour de France 2026: Tadej Pogacar wins fifth Tour as Mathieu van der Poel takes stage 21
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tadej Pogacar is considered one of the greatest riders of all timeByMatt WarwickBBC Sport Senior JournalistUp
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tadej Pogacar is considered one of the greatest riders of all timeByMatt WarwickBBC Sport Senior JournalistUpdated 1 hour agoSlovenian Tadej Pogacar won the Tour de France for a record-equalling fifth time.The 27-year-old UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider crossed the line on Paris' Champs-Elysees in the peloton, to join Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain as the endurance event's most successful male riders.All-conquering Pogacar raised the idea that his remarkable reality is proving stranger than fiction, describing it as "something you wouldn't even maybe write in a story book".The three-week Grand Tour's final stage was won by the Netherlands' Mathieu van der Poel of Alpecin-Premier Tech after a frantic charge to the line on the French capital's famous cobbles in which he pipped Denmark's Mads Pedersen by inches.Pogacar's victory means he is positioned by many as the greatest cyclist of all time, superseding the achievements and status of Belgian legend Merckx.It also marks Pogacar's third Tour win in succession and includes a record-breaking ascent of the iconic Alpe d'Huez on stage 19, when he sealed another dominant victory.It was the last of four stage wins in a race in which Pogacar used his explosive launch and unmatchable metronomic pace to see off his rivals, who for some time have had virtually no answer.Pogacar has won almost every major race in the sport, including the Tour of Flanders, Giro d'Italia, Milan-San Remo, Road World Championships, Giro di Lombardia and Liege-Bastogne-Liege.Pogacar was booed by some fans during the Tour, as his performances are often so far ahead of any of his peers that some feel frustrated the sport is losing its competitive edge.He now has 126 wins in an eight-year elite professional career."Victory is really special," said Pogacar. "Thank you to all the fans and my team."But the biggest thanks goes to all my family who support me all my life. My parents - without them I would not be standing here five times already."Seven Tours and seven times on the podium, and five wins, is something you wouldn't even maybe write in a story book, and it's unbelievable for me."It's a magnificent podium with some incredible champions to fight with."It's a shame Jonas [Vingegaard] crashed out this time and many others. I hope they have a quick recovery and next year we fight again."High drama on the Champs-ElyseesThe famous final stage, which for the overall contenders is an unchallenged formality, typically becomes a flat bunch sprint.Last year organisers ASO introduced a circuit which takes on a cobbled climb over the city's famous Montmartre hill, changing the parcours enough to encourage the heavier, more powerful riders to challenge for victory.On Sunday it was powerhouse classics legend Van der Poel who took victory after charging away with 11km remaining with Pogacar.Pogacar and Van der Poel led through the picturesque and narrow lanes over Montmartre and past Sacre-Coeur, where some fans had mobile phones knocked out of their hands as the riders squeezed past at speed, before Pogacar began to fade after three weeks of dominance and showing no weakness.Van der Poel, whose strength and staying power allow him to pull out gaps in gruelling one-day races, just managed to stay ahead of a chasing pack which included several sprinters and was rapidly closing, before he crossed the line, collapsed off his bike and lay under a barrier, breathing heavily for several minutes.Van der Poel added this prestigious victory on the famous cobbles to many of the sport's biggest one-day races, such as multiple victories in Paris-Roubaix and the Tour of Flanders.He said: "We have a saying in Dutch that it has to come for your toes. I don't know where this came from, but not from my toes."The stage was reduced from 133km to 89km after the redirection of emergency services to help tackle wildfires in south-west France.Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pogacar leads the peloton past the Arc de TriompheSlide 1 of 5, Tadej Pogacar rides past the Arc de Triomphe, Pogacar leads the peloton past the Arc de TriompheA future beyond Pogacar?The one rider who has broken Pogacar's stranglehold of cycling's biggest race in the past was Denmark's Vingegaard, who won in 2022 and 2023.But this year the 29-year-old Visma-Lease a Bike rider abandoned after breaking his collarbone on a easy right-hand bend on stage 15.The mistake was very unlike Vingegaard's near perfect technique and execution as a rider, and attention soon turned to scrutiny of the International Testing Agency (ITA), which had awoken Vingegaard at 2am to carry out an anti-doping test.Other riders had the same treatment, including Pogacar at 5am, but the ITA said there was "exceptional circumstances" to take the night tests, which are rare and require additional permission.It is not known when the test results will be published.Pogacar's only other real rival was the much-improved Belgian Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgohe, who finished six minutes 26 seconds behind overall.Third place went to Pogacar's Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro, who won stage two thanks largely to Pogacar's babysitting pace in the lead-up to the line.It would not be the only time Pogacar would aid Del Toro, 22, sacrificing his own potential victory on Saturday's brutal 'queen' stage to Alpe d'Huez to consolidate Del Toro's place on the podium.Del Toro's white jersey for the best young rider came at the expense of France's new 19-year-old star Paul Seixas of Decathlon-CMA CGM. Seixas looked stronger than Del Toro at times on the climbs but faded substantially on Saturday.Many think Seixas will be a rival to Pogacar in the future.Pidcock pleased but Netcompany without a winIn the year when Britain's four-time Tour winner Chris Froome retired, his former team - now known as Netcompany Ineos Cycling - failed to record a stage victory in 21 attempts.Ex-Ineos rider Tom Pidcock of Pinarello-Q36.5 won on Alpe d'Huez four years ago and returned to this race having achieved much with a new team built entirely around him.The 26-year-old did not manage to win a stage, but he and his team will be satisfied with Pidcock's consistent battling riding, which earned him ninth in the general classification to build on third place in last year's Vuelta a Espana.Fellow Briton Adam Yates, 33, showed great tenacity after falling ill on stage 16 and spending two days riding at the back of the field before helping pace Pogacar up a climb for victory on stage 19.Who won which jerseys?One of the most entertaining riders in the race was Ecuador's Richard Carapaz of EF Education-Easypost. He toiled earlier in the race before coming into great form to claim the king of the mountains' polka dot jersey.  He won stage 18 and Saturday's stage 20 after topping the race's highest point first and after 5,450km of climbing.The green points jersey was awarded to Pedersen of Lidl-Trek, after tenacious riding on climbs he is not typically strong on to hoover up mid-stage points, alongside winning stage four.He beat a number of sprinters to the jersey, including Japser Philipsen of Alpecin-Premier Tech. Philipsen won stage 17 and fellow Belgian Tim Merlier of Soudal-Quick Step won three bunch sprint stages.Tour de France stage 21 results1. Mathieu van der Poel (Ned/Alpecin-Premier Tech) 1hr 58mins 49secs2. Jasper Philipsen (Bel/Alpecin-Premier Tech) same time3. Mads Pedersen (Den/Lidl-Trek) 4. Max Kanter (Ger/XDS-Astana)5. Olav Kooij (Ned/Decathlon-CMA CGM)6. Matej Mohoric (Slo/Bahrain-Victorious)7. Rick Pluimers (Ned/Tudor Pro-cycling)8. Anthony Turgis (Fra/Total Energies)9. Milan Fretin (Bel/Cofidis)10. Clement Russo (Fra/Groupama-FDJ United)Tour de France general classification after stage 211. Tadej Pogacar (Slo/UAE Team Emirates-XRG) 73hrs 56mins 26secs2. Remco Evenepoel (Bel/Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) +6mins 26secs3. Isaac del Toro (Mex/UAE Team Emirates-XRG) +9mins 42secs4. Paul Seixas (Fra/Decathlon-CMA CGM) +11mins 56secs5. Lenny Martinez (Fra/Bahrain-Victorious) +13mins 2secs6. Mattias Skjelmose (Den/Lidl-Trek) +14mins 59secs7. Juan Ayuso (Spa/Lidl-Trek) +17mins 48secs8. Richard Carapaz (Ecu/EF Education-Easypost) +20mins9. Tom Pidcock (GB/Pinarello-Q36.5) +29mins 28secs10. Jordan Jegat (Fra/Total Energies) +33mins 21secs

title: Rental searches for pet friendly properties drop after law change
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentRightmove searches for rental properties that allow pets have plummeted since law changes gave
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentRightmove searches for rental properties that allow pets have plummeted since law changes gave renters more rights.Following the introduction of the new rules, pet searches dropped by more than 50% in May and June compared with a year earlier.Landlords in England cannot unreasonably refuse pets in their properties under changes made in May in the Renters' Rights Act.But agents say some renters wrongly believe permission to have a pet is guaranteed, and landlords say some homes remain unsuitable for multiple pets or large dogs."Landlords must consider requests fairly and cannot unreasonably refuse them, but they can still decline where there is a valid reason," said Megan Eighteen, former president of lettings agents trade body ARLA Propertymark.She said there was plenty of "potential for misunderstanding", among tenants about pet-friendly properties.Power shift over petsThe Rightmove data suggests that fewer tenants are proactively filtering for pet-friendly properties when searching for a home. While pets remain the most common searched-for term overall - ahead of gardens, garages and furnishings, the lead at the top is shrinking.Renter searches for properties that allow pets fell by 54% in May and 52% in June compared with the same months a year earlier, according to the figures shared with the BBC. Falls had accelerated through this year, as the changes got closer and were then introduced.Marc von Grundherr, director of agency Benham and Reeves, said some tenants have only disclosed a pet after signing their tenancy agreement, while others have been discovered during property inspections."The reality is that tenants now understand the balance of power has shifted. Landlords can no longer rely on a blanket 'no pets' policy to deter applications and should instead expect conversations around pet ownership to arise much later in the letting process," he said.Now, in England, landlords may still be able to refuse a pet if another tenant has an allergy, the property is too small for a large pet or several pets, the pet is illegal, or the landlord is a leaseholder and the freeholder does not allow pets.Before the rules changed, Eve Williamson had to give up her American Bulldog, Khan, or face eviction from her home - despite having previously had a dog in the property.The 41-year-old former hairdresser, from London, described the experience as awful, especially as Khan had brought comfort while she gave full-time care to her mum."Life can get tough, but pets bring unconditional love," she said. "They're family."Image source, Eve WilliamsonImage caption, Eve had to give up her dog - Khan - or face evictionKhan has since been happily re-homed, and Eve said she was delighted with the law change. Katie Smith, 29, from Swindon, has two cats - Pumpkin and Pippin - in her rental home. The new mum said the family had shared "wonderful moments" with pets, which would also teach children about life and death.But she said the choice of places to rent still dropped sharply on property portals when pets were part of the equation."Landlords should give them a chance," she said. Yet, even under the new rules, landlords were finding excuses to refuse potential tenants with pets, according to Russell Hunt, founder of Pets Lets, which matches clients with pet-friendly rentals.Image source, Russell HuntImage caption, Russell Hunt said landlords should consider each pet request on its meritsHe lives with a Basset Beagle cross, called Biscuit, and his three teenagers, who he jokes are more disruptive than the dog.He said pet CVs should be used and landlords should consider the circumstances more carefully, such as older dogs being calmer and sleeping more, rather than simply ruling out tenants with large or multiple pets. Cost to landlordsRepresentatives for landlords say they understand the importance of companionship that pets offer to tenants, but they can still face costly damage."Many landlords have legitimate concerns about the risk that some irresponsible pet owners pose to rental properties, or that some owners may try to keep pets in properties that are not appropriate for animals," said Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association.He said that landlords faced issues including: No power to compel tenants to take out insuranceNo legal right to request an additional depositA burden of costs should a pet cause damage to a propertyLesley Horton, the UK's chief property ombudsman said that landlords should not be levying pet surcharges as this fell outside permitted fees for issues such as late payments or lost key replacements.However, a landlord could make deductions from the tenancy deposit at the end of the tenancy for proven pet-related damage.Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell. Get in touchAre you affected by the issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: Rental searches for pet friendly properties drop after law change

title: Water returning to Gatwick Airport after major outage
description: Gatwick Airport says it is starting to see its water supply return after passengers faced long queues for toilets and closed restaurants and bars afte
body: Gatwick Airport says it is starting to see its water supply return after passengers faced long queues for toilets and closed restaurants and bars after a major supply outage.Both terminals at the UK's second busiest airport lost running water on Sunday morning after a power failure at a treatment works that serves the area.People told the BBC of confusion and frustration as all bars and restaurants were shut, some were left with nowhere to sit and waits built up outside toilets.SES Water, the company that supplies the airport, said the power outage was fixed and supplies were gradually returning, and shortly before 19:15 BST Gatwick said its water pressure was starting to return to normal. The water company, which also supplies parts of Kent, Surrey and south London, said complications caused by a power outage at Bough Beech treatment works meant some customers had experienced low water pressure or a temporary loss of supply.A spokesperson had earlier confirmed that Gatwick Airport was affected.On Sunday afternoon, SES Water said its treatment works were back up and running, but later added it would take time for the network to fully return to normal as it had been "a highly unusual and complex issue"."We want to reiterate that our teams are working as quickly as they possibly can and we are grateful for everyone's patience," the spokesperson added.Gatwick apologised and said staff had been handing out bottled water.A spokesperson added: "Our staff are on hand to support passengers and provide assistance where needed, some restaurant partners have opened to provide additional seating."Gatwick said additional teams had been deployed across both terminals to support passengers.The airport added there had been no flight cancellations as a result of the supply issues and that it was working closely with SES Water to minimise the impact."Our teams are working hard to reopen toilets and other facilities as quickly and safely as possible," a spokesperson said.BBC reporter Adam Dowling, who was flying from Valencia to Gatwick, said his flight had been delayed because of the water supply disruption and passengers had been informed that landing slots were being moved around "to reduce the number of flights" coming in to Gatwick.The BBC has contacted Gatwick Airport to confirm if there has been any flight disruption.Roger Wood, from Tunbridge Wells in Kent, said he thought his friends were joking when they told him there were no restaurants or bars open in Gatwick's south terminal.When he arrived to meet them ahead of his flight on Sunday, he found "there was no water at all - no Nando's, no Wetherspoon, all of those places were completely shut and stopping people coming in as there was no fresh water or ability to wash hands".Wood told the BBC: "The only place you could buy something was places like Pret and Itsu where it was packaged food, or shops."There was a general grumpiness and the usual frustration at not being able to get a drink at a bar from people, but everybody seemed quite resigned."Wood said people could go in the toilets but there was no way to wash hands and conditions had grown worse in the hour or two they were there.Houchin said there has been "very little information" from the airport."I think people are just fed up because they've got a long wait, but everyone understands there's nothing you can do about it," she added.Ian Bubb, who was flying to Alicante in Spain with British Airways, said there had been a "total lack of information" from the airport."Absolute disgrace at Gatwick - total lack of contingency planning for such an event," he said.The passenger said he had booked a lounge but was not allowed to sit inside.People heading to the airport for flights have been advised not to arrive early.A statement from Easyjet said: "Due to a water supply issue affecting London Gatwick Airport, bag drop desks are temporarily opening two hours before departure instead of three hours."The airline said: "Please do not arrive earlier, as you will not be able to drop off your bags or enter the departure lounge until bag drop opens."SES Water confirmed the Kent postcodes TN8 and TN11 and parts of Surrey postcodes RH1, RH6 and RH10 had no water supply or low pressure. The company said it was delivering bottled water to vulnerable customers.Gatwick Airport and the local area also suffered water issues in July 2022, when low pressure caused by a burst water main affected 1,200 houses and closed toilet facilities at the airport.

schema.headline: Water returning to Gatwick Airport after major outage

title: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lando Norris and McLaren almost perfect as Ferrari flounder
description: Lando Norris ended the first half of the Formula 1 season with a victory in the Hungarian Grand Prix that he described as "one of my best performances
body: Lando Norris ended the first half of the Formula 1 season with a victory in the Hungarian Grand Prix that he described as "one of my best performances".It was a drive that had been a long time coming, after a difficult start to the season for the reigning world champion and his McLaren team.But when McLaren finally gave him a car of the performance level he had become used to in the past season and a half, he more than made the most of it.While Ferrari, the pre-race favourites, floundered and made, in the words of their team boss Frederic Vasseur "too many mistakes", Norris and McLaren were almost perfect.Even in the context of Kimi Antonelli's stellar start to the season for Mercedes, this was one of the most impressive and convincing victories of the season.Norris' one mistake was on the first lap. He converted his pole position into a lead at the first corner, only to misjudge the grip available at Turn Two, slide wide, and gift his position to team-mate Oscar Piastri.It looked to have been a potentially fatal error to his victory hopes on a track where overtaking is all but impossible between evenly matched cars on similar strategies, but Norris stayed calm.Seeing he could easily keep pace with Piastri despite being in the dirty air, he said he always believed the win was on."It wasn't my finest Turn Two," Norris said, "but after that, seeing what my pace was like and I was just better in every sense, in terms of degradation and pace, I was convinced I could still win the race."Trapped, Norris begged for a different strategy to give himself a chance of victory, and eventually circumstances presented it to him.Around half-distance. McLaren pitted Piastri to cover off Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, which had just stopped for fresh tyres. That gave Norris clean air and he set a blistering pace.Piastri might still have held the lead, but for a collision with Carlos Sainz as he lapped his Williams. The Australian was angry after Norris came out ahead from his stop a few laps later - but at the Spaniard, not McLaren."The fact I could keep up with Oscar on this kind of track, where it's impossible to follow and impossible to overtake, I was within 0.8 seconds or something for, I don't know, almost 40 laps, the fact I could do this is what gave me confidence that I'd win the race no matter what, whether he boxed early or late or whatever," Norris said."The pace advantage I had was huge today. But I don't know why. The cars are identical, and I've just been feeling very strong lately."I've worked on many areas from last year. I feel much more confident lately with how to extract performance, and I've worked a lot with my engineers to understand this car because it's certainly not an easy car to understand and figure out how to drive on the limit consistently."So, why? Just hard work. Hard work from my engineers and from myself to improve me as a driver and improve my driving. That is the answer."Norris believes he is driving better this season than he did in the first half of his championship year in 2025.Last year, he was struggling for feeling from the McLaren.Like all his rivals, he does not like this new generation of cars as much as the last - especially their engines and the need for so much energy management, and the way they have compromised the driving experience.But he has gelled with them, while Piastri - so strong in the first half of last season - is struggling.Team principal Andrea Stella says this is a continuation of the trajectory Norris has been on since a lot of self-assessment led to his strong second half of last year, and eventually the title."Lando is much more confident. He's much more aware of his tools that he has in his driving, how to deploy these tools. And I think he's also, let me say, more in control of his emotions," Stella said."Because today, when he was behind Oscar, he said a couple of times that he had pace in hand, but he didn't get overly frustrated. And the fact that he wasn't overly frustrated, I think, then allowed him to use the pace at the right time and lead him to the victory. We've seen a great trajectory of development for Lando."This performance came after a major upgrade to the McLaren car, and there is another to come at the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after F1's four-week summer break.Norris' win moves him up to 98 points behind Antonelli, but he cautioned against expectations of a charge up to the top of the championship of the kind Max Verstappen and Red Bull mounted against him and McLaren last year."I'm just happy with today," Norris said. "It doesn't mean if I'm quick here, we're going to be quick everywhere."One thing I've learned for sure is just to have no expectations of the future and just to work in the present. I think that's the way we've been doing everything as a team."That's why we're back on top today: just working hard on ourselves as individuals and also as a team."Of course, I'm optimistic for the future and I think we can win more races, but we have good competition and there are still plenty of races I'm not confident in because the car is not to the standard that it needs to be in certain areas."During the race, it appeared as if Piastri's anger over the radio might have been partly directed at the off-set strategy that led to Norris passing him for the lead.In fact, he was instead furious with Sainz."The timing of my stop was fine," he said. "We wanted to cover off Hamilton, which was perfectly normal. Without getting crashed into, I would have been ahead of Lando still."In the moment, I was incredibly annoyed. In fact, annoyed is not the word I would use, but there was a multitude that I would, with Carlos. And, yeah, then obviously, when Lando came out ahead, I knew I had no pace to go and attack him."I knew my chances of winning the race were done from there."Discussing the collision with Sainz, Piastri added: "I don't really care if he didn't see me. The fact that he didn't and no-one told him, or there was a lack of complete awareness, is unacceptable."He's quite critical of others, and others have given him some stick before for being frustrating on track."He was not at all mollified by a problem with the GPS system that shows teams where all the cars are on track. Sainz said he had "no idea I was trying to get lapped", he "didn't expect" Piastri to be there, and it was "impossible to avoid it".For Piastri, it was academic in the end, a gearbox failure sending him into retirement and denying McLaren a one-two.As for Ferrari, they appeared to have the fastest car in Hungary, but underperformed in qualifying. Then Hamilton, after qualifying second, was dropped  to fifth on the grid with a penalty for impeding Piastri.Norris will have been worried about Charles Leclerc starting alongside him on the front row. But instead of challenging Norris, Leclerc lost out to Piastri, Verstappen and Hamilton.The seven-time champion got ahead of Verstappen in the first pit stops - only to be overtaken again the next time around, the Dutchman making a brilliant move at Turn One that caught Hamilton napping.A penalty for pit-lane speeding cost Hamilton a further five seconds, and left him behind Leclerc at the end, the Ferraris finishing fourth and fifth.Hamilton, who remains second in the championship, 50 points behind Antonelli, said "you can't make these kind of mistakes if you want to challenge for a title".Vasseur said: "It's difficult to clearly understand the pace, because I think the clean air is key, but first it's not a good Sunday, because when you are one-two on Friday, you expect much more."And on the top we made too many mistakes today, starting with the penalty and the fact that Max overtook us, that each time that we were doing a pit stop, we were losing a position for 0.2 or 0.3 seconds."And then we spent our lives behind the guys, everything went wrong, but for sure we have to do a much better job on Sunday."Norris was followed across the line by Verstappen and Antonelli, both of whom drove fine races themselves, the three podium finishers fully deserving their results.Antonelli's team-mate George Russell, meanwhile, had another day to forget. A problem with his engine at the start, for which the team took the blame, dropped him to the back at the start, and he recovered well to seventh, but still lost points to the Italian, who he now trails by 59 points."I'm sort of past the point of disappointment now, because it's just, if I'm continuing to be disappointed with everything that goes on, I'll just be disappointed every day of the week," Russell said."Obviously, another technical issue that completely ruined the race, but I can tell you some positives. The pace was very strong. "So, I'll take positives there, but yeah, it's just unbelievable, the list of things that's happened this season."Oscar had his thing today as well. It's not like we're the only one, but it does feel like it is happening substantially more to me than others, and hopefully it swings around."I don't wish any bad luck on anyone, but I've never had a season like this in my whole career, let alone my F1 career."Antonelli, then, goes off on holiday in total control of the championship. But he knows to take nothing for granted, as this time last year the same looked to be the case for Piastri."I think Lando still had the upper hand this weekend, even on us," Antonelli said."On pure pace, I don't think I would have been able to challenge him, especially with how difficult it was to follow as well, with a lot of tyre overheating."I did not expect to find myself in this position. But the car has been extremely good, the team has done an incredible job and, on my side, I try to maximise every opportunity I have."Of course, there's still lots of work to do, lots to learn, but it was a good first half of the season. Now I'm looking forward to the second half and we're just going to keep pushing."

schema.headline: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lando Norris and McLaren almost perfect as Ferrari flounder

title: It's me, Cathy – thousands pay tribute to Kate Bush classic
description: The sun may be hiding behind grey clouds, but for hundreds of people in flowing red dresses dancing on Yorkshire moorland it'll take more than a threa
body: The sun may be hiding behind grey clouds, but for hundreds of people in flowing red dresses dancing on Yorkshire moorland it'll take more than a threat of rain to dampen their spirits.This is Brontë country, after all, so it's fitting that it's also perfect Brontë weather.The group, swaying in unison, have come together to re-create the music video for Kate Bush's 1978 song Wuthering Heights, inspired by Emily Brontë's novel.Every year, thousands of people around the world don red robes – and in some cases long black wigs – for The Most Wuthering Heights Day Ever.Events have previously taken place in places such as Sydney, Copenhagen, Berlin, Folkestone and Preston.This particular "Mass Wuther" perhaps has an even stronger claim than most – it's held on Penistone Hill, not far from the famous Brontë parsonage in Haworth, in the Pennines.From the field on a clear day can be seen the ruined farmhouse of Top Withens, believed to be the inspiration for the titular farmhouse of Brontë's novel."We're really thrilled to be bringing all these people together. It's such a good-hearted, fun event. It doesn't matter whether you can dance or not," says organiser Lydia McKinnon."I just hope that the Kates and Cathys have got their thermals and their rain ponchos because they might need them."The West Yorkshire event was a sell-out in 2025, and this year the 500 tickets were snapped up within 90 seconds, according to event organisers.Proceeds are split between regional and national charities. This year, Women's Aid, Haworth and Oxenhope District Bridleways Group, and Friends of Brontë Country have been chosen.Some participants in the Mass Wuther have travelled great distances to attend – in the case of Frances Murphy and Katherine Egan, all the way from Australia. They both took part in Brisbane's event last year and said they couldn't miss the opportunity to dance in Brontë Country."It's wonderful. So many people have turned out,  and we're so lucky to have got tickets to get in," Katherine says, adding: "We love you, England."

schema.headline: It's me, Cathy – thousands pay tribute to Kate Bush classic

title: What I learned when I reopened the Lockerbie bombing files
description: I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Officials inspect the wreck
body: I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Officials inspect the wreckage of Pan Am flight 103 on 21 December 1988ByMyles BonnarBBC DisclosureUpdated 09:48 BSTI was only a year old when the UK's deadliest terror attack shocked the world.In December 1988, Pan Am flight 103 exploded - killing all 259 people on board as well as 11 on the ground in the Scottish town of Lockerbie. I was a teenager by the time Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of the bombing in 2001 and, when he later died, I thought that was largely the end of the story.It wasn't. The case still rumbles on and, later this year, a man suspected of making the bomb which blew up the plane, Abu Agila Masud, goes on trial in Washington DC.As part of a Radio 4 Intrigue podcast series, I had an opportunity to delve into this complex case with fresh eyes.The deeper I dug, the more complicated Lockerbie became and there have been times that I don't know what to believe.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was the only man convicted of the Lockerbie bombingJim Swire, on the other hand, is sure what he believes - and it is not the official story.His daughter Flora died in the bombing, but he is convinced that whoever killed her got away with mass murder.Swire believes Megrahi is innocent, even befriending the convicted bomber up until his death in 2012."The burning issue was to get to the truth," he says."Always has been, always will be and I will not shut up about what I know to be true."Swire's doggedness has made him a prominent voice but most of the Lockerbie victims' families don't agree that Megrahi's conviction was a miscarriage of justice - and the bomber’s own appeals against the verdict either failed or were abandoned.For Swire, the simplest explanation is that Iran was behind the attack - not Libya.The Lockerbie bombing came five months after 290 people were killed when an Iranian commercial airliner was shot down by a US battleship.Iran swore revenge and months later Pan Am flight 103 exploded on its way to New York.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jim Swire's daughter Flora died in the Lockerbie bombingAnd there's more.Iran - much like they do now - used proxy militant groups to pursue their ends.Before the Lockerbie bombing, a militant cell based in Frankfurt, part of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine - General Command (PFLP-GC), was foiled by German police.Police arrested suspects and seized explosive devices, concealed in radio cassette players, that were designed to trigger at altitude.The bomb that brought down Pan Am 103 was in a radio cassette player hidden inside a samsonite briefcase.Because of this, Swire believes the device that brought down Pan Am 103 was loaded at Frankfurt, and not Malta as the court had concluded.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A mock-up of the explosives-loaded Toshiba cassette recorder which blew up Pan Am Flight 103And, for Swire, this is only the tip of the iceberg.He also questions much of the evidence presented at the 2001 trial, discredits witnesses, and is extremely suspicious of the involvement of intelligence agencies - like MI5, MI6 and the CIA - in the aftermath of the bombing.Combine these suspicions with his all-consuming grief and you can see why Swire is such a force to be reckoned with on his quest for a truth he believes has been denied to him."Discovering the truth became my way of handling the consequences of the grief reaction," Swire says."And it was very tough for other people to understand that but that's just the way I'm made, I suppose."Intrigue: LockerbieOn 21 December 1988, a plane explodes over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people. Almost four decades on, there's fresh evidence. Who was really behind the bombing?Dick Marquise, who led the FBI's Lockerbie task force, says that in the early days of the case he too believed the PFLP-GC were the "number one suspect", but years of investigation found nothing to prove it."There was not one shred of evidence that could be taken to court and get a conviction," he says. "You couldn't do it. There was nothing."However, there are others, besides Swire, who still question the "official narrative" - including former CIA agent John Holt who also believes Iran was behind the bombing.Holt worked with Libyan intelligence assets in the 1980s and was the handler of double agent Abdul Majid Giaka, whose information became central to the investigation into the Lockerbie bombing.Holt now believes Giaka was a "BS artist" who was out for money and was feeding the CIA fake stories to get paid."I didn't think much of him at all," he says."He gave us some little tidbits about what was going on, but he never knew anything about the Pan Am bombing. And he knew a lot about Megrahi," Holt says.Holt believes the fact the CIA bankrolled Giaka devalues him as an informant."It makes it easier for somebody to say whatever the person who's giving them money wants them to say," Holt says.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Members of the armed forces collect debris from residential gardens after the mid-air explosion of Pan Am Flight 103I managed to get a hold of the CIA papers - known as cables - from the time, which showed what Giaka had told the Americans.The cables date back to the months before Lockerbie and include notes of conversations between Giaka and Holt and two earlier CIA handlers.Within the cables, Giaka places Megrahi in Malta - where the bomb was said to have been planted - at a key time in the Lockerbie plot.Megrahi is also said to have visited a Maltese clothes shop, buying shirts and baby grows - which were placed in the suitcase with the bomb and later found at the plane crash site.Giaka had even talked to the CIA about eight kilos of orange-coloured explosives stored at the Malta airport offices. Semtex, the explosive used in Lockerbie, is orange.In the 2001 trial, Giaka was to be a "key" witness in the prosecution's case but the four judges de­scribed some of his evidence as "at best grossly ex­ag­ger­ated and at worst sim­ply un­true".The Senussi filesDecades on from Megrahi's conviction, new intelligence documents have been recovered allegedly from the heart of Libyan intelligence.They are believed to have come from Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi's notorious intelligence network run by his spy chief Abdullah Senussi.These leaked Libyan intelligence documents contain information that could potentially put an end to the doubt, theories and countertheories that have tied so many, including me, in knots.The original 'Senussi Files', as they are now known, were shown to French journalists who later published a book, The Murderer Who Must Be Saved.I travelled to Paris to meet one of the authors, investigative journalist Vincent Nouzille.He brought piles of documents, enough to cover the whole bed and the hotel room desk.You can tell he loves his work and despite having pored over these documents for years, he's still awestruck by their content.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lockerbie bombing accused Lamin Khalif Fhimah (left) with Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi after his acquittal in 2001Some of the Senussi files date back to autumn 1988, in the months before Lockerbie, and contain documents apparently detailing plans to target aircraft on multi-stop flights using a 11-hour long-delay timer bomb concealed in luggage much like the Lockerbie bombing.It even mentions tests on concealing a device inside a tape recorder.As we go through each document, my head is spinning.There are references to dry runs, apparent weaknesses in airport security, and enough detail about the movements of Megrahi and others for Nouzille to crosscheck dates and places against other sources.Nouzille says he spent three years carefully verifying everything in the files.He shows me another file which details the apparent movements of Megrahi and Masud, coming in and out of Malta.This account lines up with the information provided in the CIA cables from the previously discredited Giaka."We know from the CIA cables that Giaka reported the same people, the same dates, the same false passport, at the same date," Nouzille says."So two sources, independent, which match."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Abu Agila Masud is accused of making the bomb that blew up Pan Am flight 103 The Senussi Files seem to corroborate several details first mentioned in the cables, including the presence of semtex at Luqa Airport in Malta.Nouzille shows me a translated document, signed by Megrahi, dated January 87, which mentions "10 kilos of explosive material" stored at the airport by Lamin Khalif Fhimah, the man who stood trial alongside Megrahi in 2001 but was acquitted.I tried to contact Fhimah via his trial lawyer to put these allegations to him, but I was unable to reach him.Nouzille concedes that these documents are not "final proof" that Libya was targeting Pan Am 103 flight, but he believes this is evidence of their modus operandi."We have a preparation of a multi-stop flight and a suitcase - and after 11 hours the bomb will explode," Nouzille says.The Senussi Files that Nouzille has are copies, not originals, so they cannot be forensically tested.It remains to be seen whether they will be admissible in the upcoming trial.If they're authentic, these files may prove once and for all that Megrahi was guilty.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Hudson, whose daughter Melina was one of the victims, holds up a banner outside the federal court in Washington DCAs Nouzille packed away the documents, I thought of Jim Swire and what this could all mean for him.He's devoted his life to this case - even befriending Megrahi during his quest to find answers.However, despite the years spent by Nouzille to authenticate the documents, the Senussi Files have failed to convince him that Libya was responsible.Swire says: "I don't think that you should, with your eyes open, go into believing that any documents, however perfect they may seem to be, are genuine which prove conveniently that this was a Libyan job."He said the CIA had the ability to forge any documents they wanted.Despite several delays, Masud is due to go on trial in August this year.Whether this will be pushed back again remains to be seen.It's very likely that historical evidence from the original Lockerbie trial will be brought under the microscope once again - opening up old wounds and catalysing a new era of questioning.Or, if admissible and verified, the Senussi Files might prove once and for all what Dick Marquise and other investigators have been saying all along.

schema.headline: What I learned when I reopened the Lockerbie bombing files

title: Burnham says he is prepared to call out Trump 'if right for Britain'
description: Image caption, Andy Burnham spoke exclusively to Laura Kuenssberg this week in his first major interview as prime minister BySunday with Laura Kuenssb
body: Image caption, Andy Burnham spoke exclusively to Laura Kuenssberg this week in his first major interview as prime minister BySunday with Laura KuenssbergAndy Burnham says he would be prepared to call out Donald Trump to defend Britain's "national interest before anything else" if it is the right thing to do, in his first major interview as prime minister.Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Burnham said he had had a good first exchange with Trump, finding him to be "really warm".But asked twice if he would trust the US president, he did not say, answering, "it's a changing world isn't it, and you just obviously have to call things as they develop".In the interview, to be broadcast in full on Monday, he said: "I can't at any point say that I won't take a different opinion from him [Trump], that I will need to voice a different idea that is right for Britain."Figure caption, Watch: 'You have to defend your own national interest before anything else'Burnham said: "My strength is remaining close to people, close to the public, that will not change as prime minister."Asked if he would call out Trump if it was the right thing, he said, "of course", going on to say: "You have to defend your own national interest before anything else. That's what you're required to do if you're to do this job properly."Burnham also said he had had "concern" about the president starting the conflict with Iran, and he "wouldn't hold back from saying what I think is right".Responding to Burnham's comments, Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: "Clearly, the US is a long standing ally. We need to have good relations with them but if they do something we disagree with, we should honestly say so."The prime minister would not commit to a date when the government would spend 3% of GDP on defence. His Chancellor John Healey resigned from the previous government saying that unless a commitment was made to spend that amount by 2030, the country would not be safe.But Burnham said: "I appointed my new chancellor very aware of what he had said about the critical importance of defence spending and the position that he had taken about that."The first challenge facing us both is to ensure that the defence investment plan is fully funded and that's the thing that's right in front of us and we need to work that through as we go towards the budget later this year."Figure caption, Watch: PM says 'we've got to work out the way' of meeting defence promisesAsked again specifically about the commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, he said: "We've got to work out the way of doing that."Burnham, for the first time, explicitly dismissed the idea of an early general election before 2029, saying: "I'm going to rule it out... I don't think people want it." He said his focus instead was on "getting the country back where it should be".Philp said the Conservatives were ready to fight an election whenever it happens."It pretty clear to me we are back in business and that the polls suggest that we are pretty much neck and neck with other parties" he said.Watch the full interview, BBC Panorama 'Andy Burnham: the Laura Kuenssberg Interview' on iPlayer from 06:00 on Monday and BBC One on Monday at 20:00 BST.

schema.headline: Burnham says he is prepared to call out Trump 'if right for Britain'

title: Aitch on reaching new heights with his Mount Kilimanjaro climb
description: How rapper Aitch's sister inspired him to climb one of the world's toughest peaksImage source, Aaron FitzmauriceImage caption, The Manchester rapper h
body: How rapper Aitch's sister inspired him to climb one of the world's toughest peaksImage source, Aaron FitzmauriceImage caption, The Manchester rapper has been pursuing challenges to raise awareness and money for the Down's Syndrome AssociationByEleanor Doyle and Naomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatHe's skydived, eaten raw fish eyes on I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! and now Aitch has reached new heights - literally - by climbing Mount Kilimanjaro.The Manchester rapper has been pursuing some of these tasks to raise awareness and money for the Down's Syndrome Association in honour of his younger sister Gracie, who has the condition. Aitch tells BBC Newsbeat the 16-year-old is an "absolute legend in the streets of Manchester" and beyond."Everyone loves her. She's just a big bottle of light in every room," he says."She's everyone's best friend and she's just got such a positive outlook on the world. "I just feel like everyone should be more like her."The musician's journey up Kilimanjaro has been captured in an upcoming Netflix documentary, Aitch: Don't Be Afraid.But he says the whole point of it was to share how having someone in his life with Down's syndrome is "one of the best things in the world".However, the 26-year-old admits he does feel "a little bit of pressure" to up the scale and fundraising targets of his challenges."You've just got to think about the end goal, which is trying to raise the most money and make the most difference to what's going on," he says.Image source, HandoutImage caption, Aitch says his sister Gracie is an "absolute legend in the streets of Manchester" and beyondHe has "smashed" his target this time by bringing in more than £160,000 so far from his climb of the highest peak in Africa. The rapper says he was able to handle the altitude and physical elements of the hike, which others in his group struggled with. But the "big mental challenge" was the biggest obstacle for him, he says.Between the early mornings, late nights and the change of climate from rainforest conditions one minute to a blizzard the next, Aitch says it was "just all a lot".He confesses the group would probably have turned around if they hadn't been doing the climb for "such a good cause".Down's syndrome is when you're born with an extra chromosome - and people with the condition are likely to have some level of learning disability.Aitch's fundraising efforts have been inspired by Gracie, who was also the subject of My G, a viral song he released in 2022. He thinks it was so popular because it showed the bond between the siblings."People love genuine things," he says."And that relationship there between me and my sister, both of my sisters, is just undeniable. Do you know what I'm saying? So I feel like that's why people loved it."Image source, Down’s Syndrome AssociationImage caption, The rapper's fundraising efforts have been inspired by Gracie, who was also the subject of his viral song My GHaving grown up as a sibling carer, Aitch has faced challenges, and seen Gracie overcome obstacles. Reflecting on how he would advise others in his position who are struggling, he says  "you've got to see the blessing in it every time". "I suppose if you ask yourself the question, 'would you change it for the world?', there's probably not a chance," he says."So it's always going to be a bit of a challenge, but sometimes you've got to just take it on the chin, keep it stepping and it'll all be all right."He also feels there is "always more that can be done" to support young carers and  improve understanding around various conditions and learning disabilities. "Where I stand, I'm trying to do what I do to raise awareness," he says. "And hopefully that brings people in. "Hopefully that makes people want to get a little bit more involved in the whole thing and just spread more awareness than ever."
